Pontius Pilate (Doctrinal)
PON-shus PYE-lit
noun
Latin Pontius Pilatus, Greek Pontios Pilatos (G4194 + G4091) — Roman prefect (procurator) of Judaea from AD 26-36 under Tiberius; the governor who authorized the crucifixion of Christ despite repeatedly declaring Him innocent. The only individual besides Christ and Mary named in the Apostles' Creed ("suffered under Pontius Pilate").

📖 Biblical Definition

Pontius Pilate is the Roman prefect (often called procurator in older texts) of Judaea from AD 26-36 under the emperor Tiberius, named in all four Gospel passion accounts (Matt 27; Mark 15; Luke 23; John 18-19) and in Acts 3:13; 4:27; 13:28; 1 Timothy 6:13. He is the only individual besides Christ and Mary named in the Apostles' Creed ("suffered under Pontius Pilate") — a deliberate historical anchor reminding the church that the crucifixion was not myth but DATED EVENT under a NAMED MAGISTRATE under a NAMED EMPIRE. Pilate's role in the Passion is theologically loaded. (1) He REPEATEDLY declared Christ innocent: "I find in him no fault at all" (John 18:38); "I have found no cause of death in him" (Luke 23:22); three times in John (18:38; 19:4; 19:6). (2) He tried to AVOID the verdict — sending Christ to Herod (Luke 23:7); offering the Barabbas-or-Jesus choice (Matt 27:17-21); proposing scourging-instead-of-crucifixion (Luke 23:16); washing his hands publicly (Matt 27:24). (3) He CAVED to political pressure when the Jewish leaders threatened "If thou let this man go, thou art not Caesar's friend" (John 19:12). (4) He nonetheless INSISTED on the trilingual placard "Jesus of Nazareth the King of the Jews" (John 19:19-22) — refusing to amend it when challenged: "What I have written I have written." Pilate is the canonical figure of UNJUST CONVICTION KNOWN AS UNJUST — a magistrate who knew Christ was innocent and condemned Him anyway under political pressure. The Apostles' Creed makes him the historical marker of the crucifixion: real governor, real date, real death.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Roman prefect of Judaea (AD 26-36) who authorized Christ's crucifixion despite repeatedly declaring Him innocent; named in the Apostles' Creed as historical anchor.

PONTIUS PILATE, noun. Roman prefect (procurator) of Judaea from AD 26-36 under Tiberius. Named in all four Gospels (Matt 27; Mark 15; Luke 23; John 18-19), in Acts 3:13; 4:27; 13:28, and in 1 Tim 6:13.

The only individual besides Christ and Mary named in the Apostles' Creed ("suffered under Pontius Pilate") — making him the historical anchor of the crucifixion as dated event under named magistrate.

📖 Key Scripture

John 18:38 — "Pilate saith unto him, What is truth? And when he had said this, he went out again unto the Jews, and saith unto them, I find in him no fault at all."

Matthew 27:24 — "When Pilate saw that he could prevail nothing, but that rather a tumult was made, he took water, and washed his hands before the multitude, saying, I am innocent of the blood of this just person: see ye to it."

John 19:19-22 — "And Pilate wrote a title, and put it on the cross. And the writing was, JESUS OF NAZARETH THE KING OF THE JEWS... Pilate answered, What I have written I have written."

1 Timothy 6:13 — "I give thee charge in the sight of God, who quickeneth all things, and before Christ Jesus, who before Pontius Pilate witnessed a good confession."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Pilate is corrupted when his hand-washing is read as effective absolution ("I am innocent of his blood" treated as actually clearing him), or when his question "What is truth?" is romanticized as philosophical curiosity rather than received as cynical dismissal of Truth standing in front of him.

expand to see more

Hand-washing absolution. Pilate's public ritual of washing his hands (Matt 27:24 — "I am innocent of the blood of this just person; see ye to it") is sometimes treated as effective absolution — as if the ritual cleansed him of responsibility. But the canonical text immediately undercuts this: the crowd accepts the bloodguilt onto themselves ("His blood be on us, and on our children," Matt 27:25), but Pilate's hand-washing does NOT actually clear him. He authorized the execution; he had the legal power to refuse and chose not to use it. "I wash my hands" became the proverbial image of evasion-without-actual-innocence precisely because of Pilate.

"What is truth?" romanticization. Pilate's question "What is truth?" (John 18:38) is often quoted as if he were a philosophical seeker. But the canonical setting is sharp: Christ has just said "Every one that is of the truth heareth my voice" — and Pilate's question is the cynical dismissal of a Roman magistrate who has heard too many religious appeals to take this one seriously. He doesn't wait for an answer; he walks out. "What is truth?" is not the question of a philosopher seeking; it is the question of a cynic dismissing Truth Himself standing in his court. The contrast with sincere seeking is total.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Latin Pontius Pilatus, Greek Pontios Pilatos (G4194 + G4091) — Roman prefect of Judaea; the magistrate who authorized Christ's crucifixion against his own verdict of innocence.

expand to see more

Greek Pontios (G4194) — Pontius; Latin Pontius, a Roman family name (gens Pontia)

Greek Pilatos (G4091) — Pilate; Latin Pilatus, possibly "armed with a javelin" (pilum)

Roman prefect of Judaea AD 26-36 under Tiberius — documented in Roman sources (Tacitus, Annals 15.44) and in the Pilate Stone inscription at Caesarea (1961)

Named in the Apostles' Creed ("suffered under Pontius Pilate") as the historical anchor of the crucifixion

Usage

"Suffered under Pontius Pilate — the Apostles' Creed's deliberate historical anchor: real governor, real date, real death."

"Pilate declared Christ innocent three times in John (18:38; 19:4; 19:6) and condemned Him anyway — the canonical figure of unjust conviction known as unjust."

""What I have written I have written" — Pilate's one act of integrity, refusing to amend the trilingual title "King of the Jews.""
